subject: Spatial Random Effect taking too much variation in model

messages.author: 399bf2e734c020dc
messages.subject: Spatial Random Effect taking too much variation in model
parts:
Hi everyone,

I am modelling fish biomass across the North Sea using a spatio-temporal tweedie georeferenced point model. I've made some very crude pictures to try and explain, in case anyone can offer some advice (code and data also attached in reply thread).



They're are regions (circled red above) that have high biomass, but these regions are predicted low biomass by the model when fitted with a fine scale prediction stack. These regions also have a high spatial correlation that has been removed by the spde random effect (also circled red, below). 



I think the spde spatial effect is removing the effect of these high biomass regions and they are not being predicted by the model, can anyone offer some advice?

Many thanks,

Sylvan

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial Random Effect taking too much variation in model
parts:
Hi,
The spde field doesn’t “remove correlation”. It captures aspects of spatial variation not captured by other components. So it seems to me what you’re showing is that if you don’t include the spde estimate in your spatial prediction, you’re missing out on biomass that isn’t explained by the rest of the model. Then, in order to produce sensible spatial predictions, you must include the spde part of the model in the spatial predictions.

But perhaps I’m misunderstanding what you’re including in your prediction expression?

(Also note that for complex observation models where predictions are needed on the observation level, not just the parameter level, one needs use posterior sampling to include the variability of the observation level as well.)

Finn

Hi Finn,

Sorry excuse me for my confusion, I thought the spde captured variation was being removed from the model. In that case, I am not sure why areas with observed biomass are being under-predicted on a fine-scale prediction grid.

Many thanks for the advice, I have not used posterior sampling before so I am not sure if I need it.

I have sent an attachment of my code if that is any interest, but my INLA call looks like this:


f4 <- response ~ -1 + intercept  + swept_area.std +
  npp.std + grav_per.std +
  vel.std + do.std +
  rock.std + mld.std +
  f(silt_grp, model="rw2", scale.model = T, constr = T, hyper = hyper) +
  f(depth_grp, model="rw2", scale.model = T, constr = T, hyper = hyper) +
  f(source, model="iid", hyper=hyper1) + f(month, model="iid", hyper=hyper1) +
  f(ship, model="iid", hyper=hyper1) +
  f(year.n, model="ar1", group = sand.n, control.group=list(model="iid"), hyper=rho.hyp2)+
  f(s.z, model=spde1, group=s.z.group, control.group=list(model='ar1', hyper=pcrho))



tweed_pred_sub<- inla(f4,
                       family=c('tweedie'),
                       data=inla.stack.data(pred.stack.z),
                       control.compute=list(dic=TRUE),
                       # fixed effect prior
                       control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 1, prec= 1),
                       control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(pred.stack.z), compute=TRUE, link=1),
                       # (strategy = "adaptive", ## faster code
                       # int.strategy = 'eb')
                       control.inla=list(int.strategy="eb", cmin=0), verbose = T,
                       safe = T)

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial Random Effect taking too much variation in model
parts:
I can’t look at the zip file until later, but the keys are likely a) what components you’re including in the prediction, and b) whether it’s spatio-temporal infill prediction or prediction into the future.

Since you showed fine scale spde field predictions that included the high values at the mentioned locations, presumably you did not include the spde component in your biomass predictions, as then it should have included those hotspot effects; it’s not clear if you included the spde component in your biomass predictions or not. If you didn’t, that’s why it underpredicts at those locations. If you did include it, then that’s a different story.

“The model” consists of the combination of _all_ your model components, so a prediction that doesn’t include the spde component shouldn’t expect to capture phenomena that the spde component was needed for.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial Random Effect taking too much variation in model
parts:
Hi Sylvan,

I think this line is your problem:
ind.predz <- inla.spde.make.index(name='pred.s.z', n.spde=mesh$n,
n.group=mesh.t$n)
Your actual spatial field component is called "s.z", so when you use
"pred.s.z" in the prediction stack, you're not linking to any actual
model component.

You should be using the exact same index object as for the estimation stack,
ind2.occ <- inla.spde.make.index(name='s.z', n.spde=mesh$n, n.group=mesh.t$n)

Finn

Hi Finn,

Yes you are right! That was my error and I had not been linking the predictions to the spde effect. However, now when running the model with the same spde index for the prediction stack the model has a problem of a negative eigenvalue and the prediction values do not make sense (up to 40000 instead of ~ 300 as before), even while using inla(.. safe=T). Do you know how I might deal with this?

*** WARNING *** Eigenvalue 5 of the Hessian is -1.51987 < 0
*** WARNING *** This have consequence for the accuracy of the hyperpar
*** WARNING *** Continue with a diagonal Hessian.

Many thanks,
Sylvan

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial Random Effect taking too much variation in model
parts:
Try
  inla.mode=“experimental”
to hopefully avoid some of the numerical issues with involving large predictions.

(Another option is to first run without prediction, and then run with predictions, but fix the hyperparameter mode as known, from the initial run)

Finn

# First run, with just the estimation stack, with unneeded posterior
integration disabled:
result1 <- inla(
...,
control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb")
)
# Second run, with the joined estimation+prediction stack, theta-mode
known from result1:
result2 <- inla(
...,
control.mode = list(theta = result1$mode$theta, restart = FALSE)
)

Finn
